answers.text: Same case as before with supplier emails. I'd tell it: give three lines always, same order — delivery date, then item and quantity, then the change from original order. This way it always looks the same, because the order stays fixed every time.
For expense claims to memo: tell it to always use date, amount, category, submitter, in that order, every time.

This looks off to me again. Call was on 14th, new date is 19th, but then it says three days from today — something isn't matching there. Price maths seems fine, 100 times 48.50. I would look into the dates before sending.
62 up from 54, about 15%, that part checks out fine. But 3 late out of 62 — that's closer to 95%, not the 97% written here. I'd flag that number to be checked.
I'd go with Output 2 again, it actually shows the two numbers, 25,100 and 612,000, so you can see the 4.1% is worked out from something real. Output 1 is just a number with nothing behind it.

I would go with Reply 2, it has the order reference and the credit reference number in it, so it's easy to check later. Reply 1 says sorry and gives a credit but there's no way to check if that 10% was actually applied or if the two-day delay is even right. That said, Reply 1 could be fine too, if someone confirms those things first before it goes out.

1. Customer's address — no, personal information, would not put that in. 2. Total sales figure — yes, that's fine, just a number. 3. Next quarter's pricing plan — no, that's not released yet, keep that out. 4. Spec sheet already on our website — not sure, maybe fine since it's already public? 5. Colleague's mobile number — no, that's personal too.

The pricing and discount numbers, I would not paste those in as they are, too sensitive for a tool we haven't cleared. The confidentiality part also, since it names both companies by name. The delivery schedule though, that seems fine to put in, nothing sensitive there.
Before the weekly report goes to my manager, I check the delivery total against my own count from that week. I do this every time before sending it on.

Step 1 carries risk because if the order details are read wrong at the start, everything after builds on that mistake. But step 4 is where it really matters, since the confirmation goes out automatically with no one checking first. I'd put the gate there, and have it flag anything where the quantity looks unusual or stock is right at the edge of what's available.
